analysis.one_liner: Bars top former officials from lobbying their old agencies for five years.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan support, never received a vote and died in the Senate committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Boren's bill would tighten the revolving door. It would make it a crime for former senior officials, including members of Congress and top congressional staff, to lobby their former agencies for years after leaving. It would also permanently bar former trade negotiators from lobbying on trade, ban former officials from being paid by foreign governments, and require violators to forfeit pay. The bill never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want government decisions made without former officials cashing in on their connections. The bill's sponsors argued it would restore public confidence that ex-officials cannot sell access after leaving office. It specifically targeted officials who left after 1993, so it applied to future officials only.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the five-year lobbying ban to the Vice President, Members of Congress, and congressional staff earning $70,000 or more, closing a gap in existing law
Bars former officials from representing foreign governments or receiving payments from them, preventing paid foreign influence
Imposes a lifetime ban on lobbying by former trade negotiators, an area where former officials routinely cash in

analysis.who_pays: Former high-level officials who might have expected lucrative lobbying careers. Lobbying firms and industries that rely on hiring former officials to gain access would face restrictions, but no specific industry is named.

drawbacks.text: The five-year lobbying ban may be an unconstitutional restriction on free speech; courts have since struck down broader versions of similar laws, suggesting the bill might have faced legal challenges
The bill covers only top-paid officials, leaving lower-level but still influential staff free to lobby immediately, so its impact is narrower than a full revolving-door ban

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real problem, the revolving door, and its targeted scope, focused on officials who left their posts after 1993, kept costs to taxpayers minimal. The main cost falls on a small group of former officials and lobbying firms. Overall it seems designed to help ordinary citizens at no cost to them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee referred it to a subcommittee, held hearings, and then the bill expired without a floor vote when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Boren introduced the bill in February 1993 with three Democratic and one Republican cosponsor
The Senate referred it to the Governmental Affairs Committee, whose oversight subcommittee held hearings in early March 1993
No further action was recorded, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former officials and lobbying firms that hire them are better off, since the stricter restrictions never became law. The public gets no protection from the practices the bill would have curtailed.

for.name: Sen. David Boren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and argued for tightening lobbying restrictions

against.name: Senate Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the Senate floor; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 1 Republican, but no vote was ever taken so no roll-call shows the final alignment.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and government relations practices
industries.note: The bill would have restricted a major revenue stream: hiring former officials to lobby their old agencies. Its failure preserves that business model.
The bill would have barred former officials from representing foreign governments or accepting payments from them, a practice that continued after the bill died.
